text:
Partnership aims to grow winter canola acres and renewable fuel supplies

Bayer and Neste have entered into a commercial agreement aimed at expanding winter canola production in the Southern Great Plains region of the United States. The collaboration is designed to help meet rising demand for renewable fuels while creating new market opportunities for farmers.

The agreement focuses on increasing the acreage of Bayer's newgold® winter canola, a crop expected to play an important role in the future biofuels supply chain. As governments, businesses, and industries seek lower-carbon energy sources, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel are becoming increasingly important. Industry estimates suggest that global demand for these fuels could grow significantly over the coming decades.

Winter canola offers several advantages for both farmers and energy producers. The crop can be planted as a rotational option alongside wheat, helping diversify farm operations and improve land use efficiency. By introducing winter canola into existing farming systems, growers may have additional opportunities to increase revenue while maintaining productive agricultural land.

The partnership also supports the development of a reliable supply of oilseed feedstocks for renewable fuel production. Oil extracted from canola can be used to produce renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. At the same time, the high-protein meal remaining after oil extraction can be used as livestock feed for dairy cattle, beef cattle, poultry, and swine.

Another important aspect of collaboration is the creation of a broader value chain network. Bayer and Neste plan to work with additional partners throughout the agricultural and energy sectors to encourage production, processing, transportation, and marketing opportunities. Building a strong supply chain can help ensure demand for growers while supporting the expansion of renewable fuel markets.

“Maximizing the contribution of novel types of raw materials to support growth in renewables requires open supply chain collaboration. By building robust value chains, we can turn agricultural innovations into scalable realities for growers and energy markets,” said Artturi Mikkola, Senior Vice President, Renewable Products Feedstock Sourcing and Trading at Neste.

HE added, “Through the Bayer newgold® winter canola collaboration, we are establishing a value chain in one of Neste’s key markets and developing opportunities to increase farm yields and grower income. This renewable raw material can be scaled rapidly in the coming years, which can help meet increasing biofuels demand.

Energy security and sustainability continue to be major priorities in many parts of the world. Renewable fuels are viewed as one practical solution for reducing emissions in transportation sectors where full electrification may be difficult. Industries such as aviation, rail transportation, marine shipping, and heavy-duty equipment often require alternative energy solutions that can work alongside existing infrastructure.

To support these growing needs, Bayer is developing new canola hybrids designed specifically for the Southern Great Plains. The company plans to introduce newgold® winter canola hybrids beginning in 2027. These hybrids are expected to offer several agronomic benefits, including improved winter hardiness, enhanced yield potential, and increased oil content.

The new canola varieties will also feature advanced trait technologies intended to help growers manage production challenges more effectively. Improved crop performance can contribute to better profitability while supporting sustainable farming practices.

For farmers, the expansion of winter canola may provide additional flexibility in crop planning. Rotational cropping systems are often used to improve soil health, manage production risks, and diversify income sources. Introducing another profitable crop option can help strengthen farm businesses while contributing to broader agricultural sustainability goals.

The growing interest in biofuels is creating opportunities across the agricultural sector. Crops such as canola, soybean, corn, and other oilseeds are increasingly being considered important components of renewable energy production. As demand rises, partnerships between agriculture and energy companies are expected to play a key role in building reliable feedstock supplies.

text:
Green hydrogen research and development (R&D) projects have been included in the Netherlands’ final, EU-approved €661m ($769m) Covid recovery package.

The cash, approved under the NextGenerationEU Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), follows the country submitting its final payment request on 2 July and will bring its total received from the fund to €3.73bn ($4.34bn).

The European Commission’s positive assessment of the request allows innovation- and education-focused initiatives advancing the adoption of green hydrogen to be eligible for a piece of the funding.

It remains unclear exactly how much of the payment could reach green hydrogen R&D, as renewable energy, energy efficiency, and tax reforms are also entitled to funds.

With the RRF set to close at the end of the year, it will be the Netherlands’ final boost from the mechanism.

The EU also recently signed off three significant Dutch state aid schemes: a $780m ($908m) initiative supporting up to 400MW of electrolysis, a €290m ($338m) hydrogen-based sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) scheme, and a €103 (€120m) clean maritime fuels investment.

Netherlands is positioned as a leader in hydrogen R&D in Europe, particularly as the host of the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research’s (TNO) Faraday Laboratory, a facility with a core focus on electrolyser technologies.

A strong network of universities, technology suppliers, and industrial users gives the country an important role within the EU’s wider push to achieve and retain technological leadership in hydrogen.

title: Biofuels Market Outlook: 5 Trends Shaping Q4 2026 and 2027 - ResourceWise
description:
What does that mean for the biofuels market in Q4 2026?
Those were among the major themes discussed during ResourceWise's latest Biofuels Market Outlook webinar.
Why Could Biofuel Demand Strengthen in Q4 2026?
Current market fundamentals point toward a strong Q4 2026 compliance environment, while higher mandates create the potential for an even stronger biofuels demand outlook in 2027.
Get the Full Biofuels Market Outlook with On-Demand Webinar These elements represent only part of the market picture discussed during ResourceWise's latest Biofuels Market Outlook webinar.
text:
Biofuel markets are heading into the final quarter of 2026 with several forces pointing in the same direction: tight diesel supply, rising compliance requirements and increasingly interconnected global trade flows.

What does that mean for the biofuels market in Q4 2026? ResourceWise expects a strong Q4 compliance environment as markets work to meet rising mandates and make up for demand that was deferred earlier in the year.

In the US, high capacity utilization and imports may be needed to balance demand. Meanwhile, developments in Europe and Asia continue to reshape global biofuel and feedstock trade.

Those were among the major themes discussed during ResourceWise's latest Biofuels Market Outlook webinar.

Key Takeaways

1. Why Could Biofuel Demand Strengthen in Q4 2026?

Some biofuel demand that might otherwise have occurred earlier in 2026 has effectively been pushed into Q4. The result is an added demand already created by rising mandates.

One important factor is the continued strength of the global diesel market. Tight diesel supply has supported high diesel prices. In turn, this provides a strong price floor for biodiesel, renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

That environment has also helped support biofuel producer margins. During the webinar, we highlighted the combination of tight conventional diesel markets and aggressive mandate growth as two important factors supporting the market through the remainder of the year.

But there is another layer to the Q4 outlook: catch-up demand.

In Europe, record heat and low rainfall pushed the Rhine to exceptionally low water levels during the summer. That made it significantly more expensive, and in some cases impossible, to move biofuels by barge from coastal production and import hubs to inland blending locations.

Read More: Record Low Rhine Water Levels Are Disrupting Europe's Biofuel Market

The result was disruption to biofuel blending and softer-than-expected demand during Q3. That demand does not necessarily disappear. Instead, some of it may move forward.

For obligated parties that still need to satisfy annual requirements, lower blending earlier in the year can mean additional volumes must be secured later. This creates the potential for Q4 compliance demand to arrive on top of an already supportive underlying market.

2. Can US Biofuel Supply Keep Pace With Demand?

The US biofuels industry may need to operate near full capacity, while imports of both biofuels and potentially feedstocks could also be needed to balance demand.

The US market illustrates just how tight the supply-demand equation could become.

ResourceWise expects the industry to need capacity utilization levels close to full through the remainder of 2026. At the same time, producers face an interesting economic decision: supplying a tight domestic market is not always necessarily the most profitable option.

US producers can manufacture fuel for domestic consumption and generate Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs). But they can also export fuel if overseas economics are sufficiently attractive, retiring the associated RINs in the process.

That means a tight domestic market does not automatically guarantee that every available gallon remains in the United States. Despite that dynamic, the broader conclusion remains the same: the US market needs substantial supply to balance its requirements.

Imports could therefore play an important role. The US will likely require biofuel imports and potentially additional feedstock imports as the market works to satisfy 2026 demand.

And the challenge does not end on December 31.

Demand requirements are set even higher for 2027, increasing the importance of production capacity, feedstock availability, and international trade as the market moves into the next compliance year.

3. Why Are Global Biofuel Trade Flows Becoming More Important?

Biofuel and feedstock markets are increasingly interconnected, meaning a supply, demand or policy change in one region can quickly influence market conditions elsewhere.

Consider the existing flow of fuels and feedstocks around the world:

The US imports feedstocks from Asia and Europe.

Europe imports renewable diesel from the US and feedstocks from Asia.

The US also imports biodiesel from Europe.

At the same time, markets including Canada, Asia and South America are developing their own demand profiles.

As domestic demand grows in those markets, volumes previously available for export may become less available to buyers elsewhere. That can alter arbitrage opportunities and put additional pressure on supply chains serving Europe and North America.

4. How Could Chinese SAF Supply Affect the European Market?

SAF provides another clear example. Growing Chinese SAF production could maintain pressure on European SAF prices as additional supply competes for demand created by Europe's aviation fuel mandates.

Chinese SAF currently faces a different European customs and trade environment than road-use HVO. As discussed during the webinar, Chinese SAF has been entering the European market in meaningful volumes.

China has substantial production capacity but comparatively limited domestic SAF demand. Additional Chinese capacity is also expected to come online.

That creates a relatively straightforward market dynamic: more supply is looking for a home.

Europe is an obvious destination. But the region's ability to absorb additional SAF remains influenced by the pace of mandated demand growth. If supply grows faster than consumption requirements, imported Chinese volumes could continue to put pressure on European SAF pricing.

This is also a useful illustration of why analyzing biofuel markets in isolation is becoming increasingly difficult.

Capacity additions in China can influence SAF pricing in Europe. European demand can affect feedstock availability elsewhere. US export economics can influence domestic RIN generation. New demand in emerging markets can reduce volumes available for established trade routes.

5. What Does the Biofuels Outlook Look Like for 2027?

Current market fundamentals point toward a strong Q4 2026 compliance environment, while higher mandates create the potential for an even stronger biofuels demand outlook in 2027.

Three factors are particularly important heading into the end of the year:

Strong diesel pricing and demand

Strong biofuel demand and pricing

Compliance shortfalls that may still need to be addressed before year-end

Together, those dynamics create a supportive setup for Q4.

But 2027 adds another consideration: mandates generally continue to increase. That means the market will need to find additional biofuel supply and the feedstocks necessary to produce it. Producers, traders, and obligated parties will also need to understand how changing regional economics affect where those volumes ultimately move.

The exact diesel-market backdrop may change, but the structural growth in mandated biofuel demand remains an important part of the equation.

OR, UNITED STATES, September 9, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- The Aviation Fuel Market is undergoing a significant transformation as rising air traffic, fleet expansion, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandates, and investments in fuel infrastructure reshape the global aviation energy landscape. The market reached USD 296.5 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from USD 324.4 billion in 2026 to USD 728.2 billion by 2035, expanding at a 9.4% CAGR. Increasing passenger travel, commercial aircraft deliveries, regulatory support for lower-carbon fuels, and investments in refining and airport infrastructure are expected to support long-term market expansion.

Aviation fuel remains essential for commercial, military, and general aviation operations. However, the industry is moving beyond conventional jet fuel toward a more diversified system that includes sustainable aviation fuel, advanced biofuel pathways, synthetic fuels, and increasingly sophisticated fuel-management technologies.

Rising Air Traffic and Fleet Expansion Drive Fuel Demand

The recovery and expansion of global air travel remain among the strongest growth drivers for the Aviation Fuel Market. Passenger numbers have recovered strongly, while airlines continue expanding fleets to serve growing demand for domestic and international connectivity. The continued delivery of narrowbody aircraft is particularly important because these aircraft account for a significant proportion of global flight frequency and fuel consumption.

The market's driver analysis identifies air traffic recovery and fleet expansion as the largest contributor to growth. Airport expansion in emerging aviation markets is also creating additional fuel demand by increasing the number of routes and aircraft movements.

Asia-Pacific is particularly important because expanding airport capacity, growing middle-class populations, and increasing airline fleet sizes are opening new aviation routes. India, China, Indonesia, and other markets are expected to contribute substantially to incremental aviation fuel consumption.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Becomes a Strategic Growth Segment

The transition toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is one of the most important structural changes affecting the industry. SAF can be produced through multiple pathways, including hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, alcohol-to-jet conversion, and Fischer-Tropsch synthesis.

Aviation biofuel is projected to grow at a 27.4% CAGR, significantly faster than conventional aviation fuel. Regulatory mandates and corporate procurement commitments are encouraging airlines and fuel suppliers to increase SAF adoption.

The shift is particularly significant because SAF allows existing aircraft and airport infrastructure to use lower-carbon fuel blends without requiring a complete replacement of the global aviation fleet. As blending requirements become more stringent, refiners and fuel suppliers are expected to increase investment in production capacity, feedstock sourcing, certification, and distribution infrastructure.

Jet A and Jet A-1 Continue to Dominate

By fuel type, Air Turbine Fuel, including Jet A and Jet A-1, accounted for approximately 88.1% of market value in 2025. Their dominant position reflects widespread fleet compatibility, established refinery capacity, and extensive airport distribution infrastructure.

SAF is growing rapidly from a smaller base, while aviation gasoline remains important for piston-engine aircraft and flight training. Aviation gasoline is valued at approximately USD 3.1 billion, supported by general aviation requirements.

Conventional kerosene is expected to remain the foundation of the aviation fuel system throughout the forecast period. However, its relative share is likely to decline gradually as blended SAF volumes increase.

Commercial Aviation Leads End-User Demand

Commercial aviation represented approximately 74.2% of Aviation Fuel Market demand in 2025, making it the dominant end-user segment. Passenger traffic growth, fleet expansion, and increasing flight frequency are the primary factors supporting this position.

Military aviation represents another significant demand center, with approximately USD 51.8 billion in 2025 procurement value. General and business aviation is projected to grow at a 6.1% CAGR, supported by fractional aircraft ownership, charter operations, private aviation, and specialized flight activities.

Narrowbody Aircraft Represent the Largest Aircraft Segment

Widebody aircraft generated approximately USD 91.4 billion, supported by long-haul passenger services and cargo operations. Regional aircraft are projected to grow at a 5.9% CAGR, with connectivity programs in markets such as India and Brazil supporting demand.

Rotorcraft represent a smaller portion of total demand but remain important for offshore energy, emergency services, defense, and specialized aviation applications.

Airport Fuel Infrastructure Creates New Opportunities

Airport fuel distribution infrastructure is becoming increasingly important as fuel suppliers introduce higher volumes of blended and sustainable aviation fuels.

Airport hydrant systems accounted for 63.7% of distribution-channel demand in 2025, reflecting their efficiency at large international airports. Refueller trucks and bowsers remain important at secondary airports and locations where dedicated hydrant systems are unavailable.

Pipeline-to-terminal distribution is projected to grow at an 8.4% CAGR. Investments in pipelines, storage terminals, blending facilities, and hydrant upgrades can improve fuel supply security while supporting the introduction of new fuel types.

Infrastructure development is therefore becoming a competitive factor alongside fuel production capacity.

North America Holds the Largest Regional Share

North America accounted for approximately 33% of the Aviation Fuel Market in 2025, supported by its extensive domestic aviation network, high passenger traffic, established refinery infrastructure, and investment in SAF production.

The United States represents the largest market within the region, supported by substantial commercial aviation activity and government incentives for lower-carbon fuel production. Refinery conversions and Gulf Coast investments are also strengthening the region's position in SAF supply.

Europe represents another major market, with approximately USD 65.2 billion in value. Regulatory requirements for SAF blending and carbon reduction are important drivers of investment.

Asia-Pacific Is the Fastest-Growing Region

India is particularly attractive, with its aviation fuel market projected to grow at a 13.9% CAGR. The country's expanding airline fleet, connectivity initiatives, airport development, and large aircraft order backlog provide strong long-term demand potential.

China also represents a major market due to the scale of its domestic aviation network and increasing aircraft utilization. Japan and South Korea are investing in SAF and fuel-conversion initiatives, while Southeast Asian countries are developing aviation infrastructure and sustainable fuel capabilities.

Feedstock Availability Remains a Major Challenge

Despite the rapid development of SAF, feedstock availability is a significant constraint. Used cooking oil, tallow, and other waste lipids are already heavily demanded by renewable diesel producers. Competition for these feedstocks can increase costs and restrict the expansion of lipid-based SAF production.

This limitation is encouraging investment in alternative pathways such as alcohol-to-jet, cellulosic fuels, and power-to-liquid technologies. Diversifying feedstock sources will be essential for meeting long-term SAF blending requirements.

The industry must also address the capital intensity of synthetic fuel production. Power-to-liquid projects require significant investment in renewable electricity, hydrogen production, carbon capture, and fuel synthesis.

Digitalization Improves Fuel Management

Fuel suppliers and airlines are increasingly using digital technologies to improve fuel procurement and operational efficiency. AI-based tankering optimization can evaluate fuel prices, aircraft weight, route requirements, and airport availability to reduce unnecessary fuel carriage.

Real-time fuel-quality monitoring, density measurement, hydrant analytics, and automated inventory management are also creating opportunities for aviation fuel companies to move beyond traditional commodity distribution.

As fuel margins become increasingly competitive, digital services can provide additional revenue streams while helping airlines reduce operating costs.

Emerging Opportunities in Synthetic Aviation Fuel

Power-to-liquid technology represents a long-term opportunity for the Aviation Fuel Market. Regions with abundant low-cost renewable electricity and concentrated carbon dioxide sources could become important centers for synthetic aviation fuel production.

Electrolyzer cost reductions and expansion of renewable energy capacity could improve the economics of synthetic fuels. Locations in Chile, Morocco, Australia, and the Middle East are attracting interest because of their renewable-energy potential.

Existing refineries also offer opportunities for conversion. Retrofitting hydroprocessing assets can potentially bring sustainable fuel production online faster and at lower cost than constructing entirely new facilities.

Lifecycle carbon intensity and traceability are becoming strategic factors in aviation fuel procurement. Airlines, corporations, regulators, and fuel suppliers increasingly need reliable information about the emissions associated with fuel production and transportation.

Book-and-claim systems are emerging as another mechanism for supporting SAF adoption. These systems allow environmental attributes to be separated from physical fuel delivery, enabling corporate customers to account for SAF-related emissions reductions even when physical fuel is consumed elsewhere.

Consequently, carbon data, verification, certification, and traceability are becoming valuable components of the aviation fuel supply chain.

text:
The aerospace, aviation and airline sectors generate £11.5 billion in economic value for South West England each year, according to new analysis from industry body Sustainable Aviation.

The report places the region among the UK’s leading aviation hubs, with major employers including Airbus, GKN Aerospace and Bristol Airport. highlights aviation’s major role in supporting jobs and economic growth across South West England.

Duncan McCourt, Chief Executive of Sustainable Aviation, said: “From Cornwall to North Somerset, these findings show that aviation is a major driver of economic growth and employment across South West England. Every year, the sector contributes more than £11 billion to the regional economy and supports over 89,800 jobs.

“The benefits of aviation are felt far beyond aviation. It connects businesses to customers and markets around the world, supports key industries, attracts inward investment and tourism and helps people stay connected with friends and family. It is one of the UK’s most important sectors, delivering growth and innovation directly and enabling growth in other sectors.

“As we continue to decarbonise, this economic contribution underlines why aviation is such an important enabler and why we should support the sector to be globally competitive.”

How wider economic benefits are generated across the entire region

Across the whole of South West England, aviation is a driver of growth and jobs:

• North Somerset, Somerset and Dorset generates almost £2.8 billion GVA and aviation is responsible for more than 23,159 jobs.

• West of England generates almost £3.6 billion GVA and aviation is responsible for more than 27,387 jobs.

• Gloucestershire and Wiltshire generates almost £2.4 billion GVA, and aviation is responsible for more than 18,512 jobs.

Nationally, UK aviation and aerospace contributes more than £100 billion to the UK economy every year and employs nearly one million people. The new report, ‘Economic contribution of aviation to the UK economy’ produced by Steer for Sustainable Aviation, assesses the impact of the UK’s aviation sector across three core industries, airlines, airports and aerospace. It measures the sector’s direct economic activity, as well as the wider contribution generated through supply chains and employee spending across the latest data available.

Why investment in innovation and sustainability is essential to maintaining the growth trajectory

Sustainable Aviation also recently published its 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map, which sets out the progress already made to decarbonise the sector and how it can continue to reduce emissions, dependent on the right policy support, investment and actions across government and industry.

John Copley, Chief Operating Officer at ADS, said: “This report is a powerful reminder that aerospace is not only essential to connecting people, businesses and markets but also a major driver of economic growth and prosperity.

“Crucially, maintaining and growing this contribution will depend on continued investment in the technologies and innovations that will shape the next generation of aircraft. From more efficient and lower-emission airframes and propulsion systems to advanced manufacturing and digital technologies, the UK’s aerospace sector has a pivotal role to play in delivering both economic growth and the industry’s long-term sustainability ambitions.

“The report highlights that aerospace alone contributes significantly to the UK economy, underlining the strategic importance of maintaining the UK’s position as a global leader in aerospace innovation. By backing industrial capability, we can ensure the UK remains at the forefront of aviation’s future while securing highly skilled jobs and investment for decades to come.”

Opening up economic opportunities and new markets for British businesses

Karen Dee, chief executive of AirportsUK, the trade body for UK airports, said: “This report provides more excellent data on the vital impact of airports and wider aviation on the economy, creating jobs and wealth through connecting the UK with the world.

“We can increase this impact through sustainable growth, providing travellers and businesses with more choice and competition, while also making good on our net zero commitments.

“It is now up to the sector and government to work together to deliver this prosperity for the whole of the UK.”

Tim Alderslade, Chief Executive of Airlines UK, the trade body for UK Airlines, said: “UK airlines are part of an aviation and aerospace success story that brings benefits to all parts of the country. Not only do airlines support hundreds of thousands of jobs, they also underpin our tourism and travel industries and open up new markets for UK businesses.

“By working with government to realise our commitment to a more sustainable future, including by using sustainable aviation fuels that are already making a difference today, we can grow these benefits long into the future.”

text:
National, September 9, 2026: Akasa Air, India’s fastest-growing airline, successfully operated a commercial flight using conventional aviation turbine fuel blended with 1% Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), supplied by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) on September 8, 2026. The flight departed Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, Mumbai, at 13:05hrs IST and arrived at Manohar International Airport (GOX), Goa, at 14:30hrs IST.

The initiative builds on the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Akasa Air and BPCL in July 2026 to explore adoption of SAF, along with other opportunities supporting aviation decarbonisation. The flight will provide both organisations with insights and practical learnings that can help inform future initiatives.

Commenting on the milestone, Ankur Goel, Chief Financial Officer, Akasa Air, said, “Sustainability is one of Akasa Air’s core values and shapes how we are building the airline for the long term. Since inception, we have invested in next-generation aircraft, technology and responsible practices that enable more conscious and efficient operations, both on the ground and in the air. This flight with BPCL translates our partnership into tangible action. Scaling SAF in India will require coordinated action across the ecosystem, supported by domestic supply, enabling policy and commercial viability. We are committed to exploring this transition.”

The flight comes as India works towards its ambition of achieving 5% SAF blending by 2030 and reflects the aviation industry’s broader focus on reducing carbon emissions. It also contributes to the International Air Transport Association’s goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Sustainability has been embedded in Akasa Air’s ethos since inception, with the airline continuing to implement initiatives focused on conscious and efficient operations.

Akasa Air’s brand-new Boeing 737 MAX fleet is a key enabler of its mission to operate one of the most environmentally progressive and fuel-efficient fleets in the Indian skies. Powered by CFM International LEAP-1B engines and incorporating advanced-technology winglets, the 737 MAX offers excellent economics, reducing fuel use and emissions by 20 per cent compared to the airplanes it replaces. The airline has also partnered with OpenAirlines to implement SkyBreathe®, a cutting-edge fuel management solution that uses advanced analytics to reduce carbon emissions and enhance operational efficiency across the network. Akasa Air was the first Indian airline to voluntarily opt out of traditional water-cannon salutes at route inaugurations, conserving over 5,50,000 litres of water to date.

text:
Japan has issued the first certificate under ClassNK SCS, Asia’s first sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) certification scheme approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). The first certification marks the scheme’s full operational launch and provides Japanese producers with a domestic pathway to demonstrate SAF compliance with CORSIA requirements.

The first certificate was awarded to Japan’s Mokukan no Mori, a Sumitomo Forestry Group company involved in the use of woody biomass resources. The new scheme therefore covers, among other pathways, supply chains using wood-processing residues as feedstock.

ClassNK SCS was approved by ICAO in October 2024 as the world’s third and Asia’s first SAF certification scheme. Its launch allows Japanese companies to obtain certification through domestic bodies under a framework aligned with national laws and business practices, whereas producers previously relied largely on overseas certification schemes.

Certification is a key requirement for SAF to qualify under the international CORSIA framework. For fuel to be recognized as CORSIA Eligible Fuel, relevant participants throughout the supply chain must meet certification requirements. The availability of an Asia-based scheme should make it easier to develop regional SAF production and supply chains.

ClassNK plans to expand its network of certification bodies and develop the scheme as part of SAF certification infrastructure not only in Japan but across Asia. This could support greater supplies of sustainable aviation fuel and broaden the range of feedstocks used in its production.

title: South Korea's GS Caltex to Supply 2000 Tons of Sustainable Aviation Fuel to DHL Express
description:
GS Caltex is expanding the scope of its biofuel business by supplying sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to the international express delivery company DHL Express.
The signing ceremony was attended by Kim Chang-soo, Vice President of GS Caltex's Mobility & Marketing Division, and John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express.
Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply SAF to aircraft that DHL Express refuels in South Korea over the next year.
Co-processing SAF supply using its own refinery processes also began in earnest in 2024.
By securing ISCC EU certification, GS Caltex has established a system capable of supplying products that meet European standards.
text:
GS Caltex is expanding the scope of its biofuel business by supplying sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to the international express delivery company DHL Express. The two companies signed a partnership memorandum of understanding for SAF-based carbon reduction on the 8th at GS Tower in Seoul's Gangnam district. The signing ceremony was attended by Kim Chang-soo, Vice President of GS Caltex's Mobility & Marketing Division, and John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express.

Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply SAF to aircraft that DHL Express refuels in South Korea over the next year. The supply volume is 2,000 tons on a neat SAF basis, before blending with conventional jet fuel. The product is manufactured using a co-processing method, in which petroleum-based feedstock and animal- and plant-based bio-feedstock are fed together into existing refinery equipment. It has obtained ISCC EU certification, which complies with the European Union's Renewable Energy Directive.

The collaboration between the two companies extends beyond fuel supply. GS Caltex has also agreed to participate in DHL Express's "GoGreen Plus" program. This service, which supports carbon emission reductions in the transportation process based on SAF usage, will be applied to all goods that GS Caltex ships internationally through DHL Express going forward.

Production infrastructure expansion is also accelerating in line with supply growth. GS Caltex plans to build dedicated bio-feedstock tanks and dedicated pipelines connecting to refinery processes by year-end, establishing a dedicated co-processing SAF production line. Through this, the company aims to secure commercial-scale SAF production capacity and respond to market demand.

A GS Caltex official said, "With this SAF supply to DHL Express, we have taken another step forward in expanding our customer base," adding, "We will continue to expand our biofuel business, including SAF, in line with market demand."

SAF Business Expansion History

GS Caltex's SAF business has progressed in stages over recent years. In 2023, the company participated in biofuel demonstration research led by South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, sourcing SAF from the Finnish biofuel producer Neste. In September of the same year, GS Caltex began SAF refueling and pilot flights with Korean Air, completing a total of six pilot flights.

In September 2024, the company exported a blend of Neste's neat SAF with conventional jet fuel to Narita Airport through Japan's Itochu Corporation. The company assessed this as the first case of a South Korean refiner selling ISCC CORSIA-certified SAF at commercial scale.

Co-processing SAF supply using its own refinery processes also began in earnest in 2024. GS Caltex has sequentially supplied SAF to Asiana Airlines, Jin Air, and Eastar Jet starting December 2024, to Korean Air starting September 2025, and to Aero K Airlines starting December of the same year.

Engagement with the Global SAF Market

The agreement with DHL Express is significant in that GS Caltex has expanded its customer base from a focus on South Korean airlines to an international express logistics network. DHL Express is a global express delivery company operating in more than 220 countries and territories, and has been expanding SAF procurement to reduce carbon emissions in air cargo transportation.

The European Union has been implementing the ReFuelEU Aviation regulation since 2025, which mandates a certain percentage of SAF blending by aviation fuel suppliers. In Asia, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea have also set SAF usage targets, with demand growing rapidly. By securing ISCC EU certification, GS Caltex has established a system capable of supplying products that meet European standards.

GS Caltex's construction of a dedicated co-processing production line is interpreted as an investment to respond to this growing global demand. The co-processing method, which utilizes existing refinery equipment, has the advantage of relatively low initial investment burden since SAF can be produced without large-scale new facilities. However, securing a stable supply of bio-feedstock and technical optimization of the refining process remain key challenges.

title: Farnborough International Airshow celebrates 78th birthday - ADS Advance
description:
To mark 78 years since the first Farnborough International Airshow, here’s a closer look at the first Farnborough airshow – and how it laid the foundations for one of aerospace’s most influential industry events.
From UK aircraft showcase to international event The roots of Farnborough International go back to the Society of British Aircraft Constructors (SBAC), which had staged aviation exhibitions before the Second World War.
Farnborough International Airshow: Where aircraft history was made For aerospace enthusiasts, Farnborough’s history is packed with memorable aircraft and demonstrations.
The 2026 Farnborough International Airshow attracted 141,580 trade and public visitors from 136 countries.
What’s next at Farnborough International Airshow?
text:
Farnborough has been a fixture of the UK aerospace industry for 78 years, evolving from a showcase for Britain’s post-war aircraft manufacturers into a major international marketplace for aerospace, defence and space.

The show has changed dramatically during that time, but its role as a place where industry meets, deals are done and new technology is put in front of the world has remained consistent.

To mark 78 years since the first Farnborough International Airshow, here’s a closer look at the first Farnborough airshow – and how it laid the foundations for one of aerospace’s most influential industry events.

From UK aircraft showcase to international event

The roots of Farnborough International go back to the Society of British Aircraft Constructors (SBAC), which had staged aviation exhibitions before the Second World War.

After the war, the SBAC shows returned at Radlett in Hertfordshire. Yet the rapidly developing British aircraft industry needed more space, meaning attention turned to Farnborough.

The Hampshire site already had a significant place in aviation history. It was home to the Royal Aircraft Establishment and had been associated with some of Britain’s earliest aviation experiments.

The first Farnborough show ran from 7-12 September 1948, with 66 British aircraft on display. This gave visitors a chance to see the latest developments from an industry that was central to Britain’s post-war industrial ambitions.

Foreign participation increased during the 1960s and, in 1962, the decision was taken to move to a biennial format. Farnborough was increasingly becoming an international aerospace showcase rather than an event focused solely on British manufacturers.

The commercial side of the show continued to develop, too. Farnborough International Limited was established in 1974, providing the organisation behind the event with a more defined commercial footing.

Farnborough International Airshow: Where aircraft history was made

For aerospace enthusiasts, Farnborough’s history is packed with memorable aircraft and demonstrations.

In 1958, the RAF’s Black Arrows flew a record-breaking formation loop involving 22 Hawker Hunters. The display remains one of the most famous moments in the show’s history. And then came Concorde.

The prototype made its Farnborough debut in 1970, providing a glimpse of what supersonic passenger travel could look like. It was one of many aircraft that used Farnborough as a platform to demonstrate what the industry could achieve.

Over the years, the show has also hosted major appearances from aircraft including the Vickers VC10, Eurofighter Typhoon, F-35 Lightning II and Airbus A380.

But while the aircraft have always attracted attention, the business taking place behind the displays has become increasingly important.

Where business meets innovation

For today’s aerospace and defence sector, the show has become a place for manufacturers, suppliers, governments, armed forces, airlines and investors to meet. Aircraft and engine orders attract the headlines, but the event also provides opportunities for companies across the supply chain to develop relationships and showcase their capabilities.

That is particularly significant for the UK’s aerospace and defence sector.

Farnborough provides British businesses – from major primes to specialist SMEs – with an international shop window. For smaller companies, being part of that ecosystem can provide opportunities to meet potential customers, partners and investors from markets that would otherwise be difficult to access.

Farnborough in numbers

The scale of the event today is a long way from those 66 aircraft displayed in 1948.

The 2026 Farnborough International Airshow attracted 141,580 trade and public visitors from 136 countries. Across the four trade days, £62.9 billion ($84.9 billion) of deals were announced, including 353 firm aircraft orders and 904 firm engine orders. More than 63% of exhibitors were international.

A sixth exhibition hall was also added for 2026 after exhibition space sold out ahead of the show, making it the largest Farnborough to date.

The changing landscape of Farnborough Airshow

Today’s aerospace and defence industry spans everything from advanced manufacturing and propulsion to autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, space technology and new forms of electric flight.

That changing landscape was visible at the 2026 show.

Vertical Aerospace carried out what Farnborough organisers described as the first public eVTOL flight at the event, bringing a very different type of aircraft into the flying display.

At the same time, defence and space remained central to the show, with major programmes and technologies attracting attention from governments and industry.

For the UK supply chain, that broadening of Farnborough’s remit matters. Companies that might once have considered themselves outside the traditional aerospace sector can increasingly find a place within the wider ecosystem.

What’s next at Farnborough International Airshow?

So what will shape the next 78 years at Farnborough – and beyond?

Decarbonisation, sustainable aviation fuel, hydrogen, hybrid and electric propulsion are likely to shape the future of civil aerospace, while defence investment is driving development in areas such as autonomous systems, uncrewed aircraft, advanced sensors and next-generation combat capabilities. Space is also firmly established within the wider Farnborough story too.

Meanwhile the industry needs to attract and develop the engineers, technicians, designers and other specialists who will build the next generation of aerospace and defence technology. Initiatives such as Pioneers of Tomorrow are part of Farnborough’s role in connecting young people with the sector and showcasing the range of careers available.

The technology has changed beyond recognition, but the basic idea has survived for 78 years: bring the industry together, show what is possible and give businesses a platform to build what comes next.

With the approval, Belgium has joined the growing number of European countries where Sunoil can sell its biodiesel made from waste materials.

Sunoil produces biodiesel from certified waste oils and fats at its facilities in Emmen and Kampen. The company also operates a trading business in Amsterdam.

Its biodiesel is used as an alternative to fossil-based diesel or mixed with fossil diesel for use in road transport, shipping and the energy sector.

Free for nonsubscribers

By Charles Alcock

Sept. 8, 2026, (c) Leeham News: As the Iran war enters its seventh month, airlines are still pondering the best—or perhaps least bad—response to the Middle East market disruption, according to the latest analysis from London-based consultancy IBA.

In a briefing on Sept. 4, the IBA team indicated that, for now, carriers are largely still focused on tactical decisions related to the crisis, which chief economist Stuart Hatcher concluded has proved to be “not quite as bad as you might think.”

“No one is looking at this in a super long-term way, given that the situation was expected to be short-term at the outset,” Hatcher reflected. “Generally, [airline seat] capacity has recovered since August, after five months of being negative.”

That said, IBA said that carriers are now facing longer-term decisions as to when to place planned fleet orders against a backdrop of stubbornly high, margin-suppressing fuel prices. They are also in touch with lessors about how they could obtain newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft more quickly and how they might get reductions on lease rates.

Last week, crude oil barrel rates fluctuated by $20 in further signs of energy insecurity triggered by new attacks and counterattacks between U.S. and Iranian forces. This week has brought the added element of conflict between Houthi forces in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

According to IBA, the crack spread—the differential between crude oil prices and the cost of refined products like Jet A—is now between four to seven times higher than the long-term base rate. “Prolonged exposure to these costs for carriers using older aircraft prolongs the pain, because [fuel price] hedging won’t last indefinitely.”

These factors were reflected in airlines’ second quarter results, according to IBA’s head of consulting Dan Taylor, who said that operating margins showed decline after the first four months of the conflict, with carriers outside the region having to contend with disruption to long-haul routes. The degree to which airlines have been able to hedge on fuel pricing was once of the main variances, he observed. While North American airlines having mainly been less exposed to fuel price spikes, they are generally less hedged and so this could catch up with them in the absence of a permanent and complete reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, IBA anticipates airlines will conduct further fine tuning across their networks to deploy more efficient equipment on longer sectors. More of the Europe-Asia traffic is now avoiding the Gulf, where traffic volumes remain at least 3.5 % down, and African traffic volumes have also taken a hit.

“The financials will continue to look worse due to fuel prices and also inflationary pressure from maintenance and employee costs,” Taylor said. “Overall, the risk outlook is deteriorating.”

In the still-longer term, IBA sees what it calls aviation’s “climate transition” toward imposed reductions in carbon dioxide and other emissions as another key concern for airline leaders.

“Climate risk will become capital risk throughout the value chain, and are clients are now worrying about this,” Taylor explained.

Pressure to replace fuel-inefficient older aircraft will raise new doubts about the value durability of these assets. But beyond that, IBA expects that airlines will need to confront higher liability from complying with green aviation mandates, such as increased use of sustainable aviation fuel, especially beyond 2030 when mandates harden and free allowances disappear.

The Hong Kong-based airline says the real reason for cutting contrails has nothing to do with conspiracy theories.

text:
Cathay Pacific has announced a partnership with Google to research and trial artificial intelligence tools designed to help its pilots avoid creating contrails, the white streaks that trail behind aircraft at high altitude. Those same streaks have long fueled the "chemtrails" conspiracy theory, which claim planes spray chemicals into the atmosphere.

The Hong Kong-based airline says the real reason for cutting contrails has nothing to do with conspiracy theories. Contrails, short for condensation trails, form when hot engine exhaust meets cold, humid air at cruising altitude. Scientists estimate contrails account for roughly one-third of aviation's total climate impact, according to assessments Google attributes to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, because persistent contrails can spread into cloud-like formations that trap heat in the atmosphere.

Early Results: A 40% Reduction

Cathay Pacific and Google began an operational trial in late 2025, targeting more than 100 flights across Cathay's network. Of those, more than 80 flights followed contrail-avoidance routing, and Google's satellite imagery analysis estimated that these flights reduced the warming impact of their contrails by roughly 40%.

Following those results, Cathay Pacific and Google are now scaling into a larger second phase of trial flights and have brought on Contrails.org, a nonprofit focused on advancing the science of contrail mitigation, as a partner.

How the AI Tool Works

The system pairs Cathay Pacific's flight data with Google's AI models, satellite imagery, and weather intelligence to predict which sections of airspace are most likely to produce persistent contrails on a given day. Flight dispatchers cross-reference those predictions with intended flight plans and revise them as needed, sometimes through minor altitude adjustments, before handing the updated plans to pilots. The forecasts are delivered through Cathay's Electronic Flight Folder system and update dynamically via in-flight Wi-Fi, keeping pilots current on changing conditions.

In practice, avoiding a contrail-forming zone might mean flying a few thousand feet higher or lower than originally planned. The change is small, but the climate benefit could be significant if the approach is proven and scaled across a full network.

Cathay Pacific is Google's first commercial airline partner in the Asia-Pacific region to trial this contrail mitigation technology, and the first airline globally to test contrail avoidance specifically on ultra-long-haul flights – defined in the partnership's announcement as routes of more than 16 hours and often 13,000 kilometers or more. Google has previously run similar contrail-avoidance projects across U.S. airspace and the North Atlantic, though specific comparative results from those earlier trials were not detailed in this announcement.

The Chemtrails Connection

The white lines produced by jet engines have been a fixation for conspiracy theorists for decades. Believers argue the trails contain harmful substances deliberately released for purposes ranging from weather control to population management. Scientists and aviation regulators have repeatedly rejected these claims, explaining that contrails are simply ice crystals formed from water vapor in engine exhaust.

Part of a Broader Sustainability Push

The contrail research fits into Cathay Pacific's wider environmental strategy. The airline has committed to reaching net zero carbon emissions by 2050 and plans to use sustainable aviation fuel for 10 percent of its total fuel consumption by 2030. Reducing carbon emissions remains Cathay's primary climate focus, through fleet modernization, operational efficiency improvements, and greater SAF adoption – the airline has been clear that contrail avoidance complements, rather than replaces, those longer-term investments, since avoiding contrails does not offset the carbon released when aircraft burn fuel.

Lawrence Fong, Director Digital and IT at Cathay Pacific, said the partnership reflects the airline's interest in solutions that can be deployed with existing aircraft.

Aviation needs solutions to address climate change, and AI is accelerating that progress,

Fong said.

This partnership combines Cathay's operational expertise with Google's world-class AI capabilities to tackle complex sustainability challenges at scale.

Google Hong Kong Managing Director and General Manager Michael Yue said the partnership is researching how predictive AI could be deployed in live operations "to help address the climate impact of contrails with today's aircraft and today's fuel."

Google, for its part, has been building out its contrail-forecasting research for several years, using machine learning trained on satellite imagery to identify where and when contrails form. That data feeds prediction models that airlines can integrate into flight planning software.

What Happens Next

Cathay Pacific and Google have not disclosed a precise timeline for concluding the expanded second-phase trials, but the companies said the work will help build a broader understanding of how contrail avoidance could function across different Asia-Pacific and transpacific operating environments, and inform whether the approach can be implemented and managed at scale across the aviation industry.

Background The Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit, as modified by the WFTC, provides a tax credit for eligible clean transportation fuels produced domestically and sold in a qualified sale, including sustainable aviation fuel and other clean fuels.
The credit amount generally depends on a fuel's lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate, with lower-emission fuels qualifying for larger credits.
The guidance provides for distinct emissions rates for transportation fuel derived from specific animal manure feedstocks, as required by the WFTC.
The 2026 emissions rate table includes dairy manure and swine manure, and Treasury and IRS anticipate that the 45ZCF-GREET model will be updated later in 2026 to include poultry manure and beef manure as primary feedstocks.
text:
IR-2026-108, Sept. 8, 2026

WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service today issued guidance on the Section 45Z Clean Fuels Production Tax Credit to empower America’s crop and livestock farmers, ranchers, and fuel producers across the country and help them access the growing domestic biofuels market in a way that makes the Clean Fuels Production Credit work for them.

“Today's guidance helps America’s farmers, ranchers, and fuel producers access growing opportunities in the domestic biofuels market,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano. “This guidance helps unlock billions of dollars for America’s agricultural producers, provides greater certainty for investment across rural America, strengthens domestic biofuel production, and helps lower fuel costs for American consumers.”

Notice 2026-53 PDF provides the 2026 emissions rate table used to calculate the clean fuel production credit and provides additional guidance, including on the use of manure-derived fuels and regenerative agricultural practices, supporting American biofuel production.

Notice 2026-53

The Working Families Tax Cuts (WFTC) amended and extended section 45Z, including making several changes that require technical modeling updates to the 45ZCF-GREET model used to determine emissions rates. The section 45Z proposed regulations, which were issued February 4, 2026 and are under final consideration by the IRS and Treasury Department, proposed rules implementing the WFTC changes to the Clean Fuels Production Credit, including addressing how the annual emissions rate tables work and which table and models a producer should use to determine the emissions rate of a particular fuel.

Today’s notice provides certain technical modeling language used to implement WFTC-mandated model updates for manure-derived fuels. This notice addresses how producers should account for WFTC changes when using the emissions rate table and allowed models. The DOE is developing corresponding updates to the 45ZCF-GREET model.

The 45Z proposed regulations indicated that the IRS would provide further guidance on how United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) rules on regenerative agricultural practices will be integrated into the 45ZCF-GREET model once the USDA finalized its rules, which USDA did on June 29, 2026. This notice provides a safe harbor that will be available for 2025 clean fuel production.

The notice also provides transition rules for applying changes made by the WFTC when an allowed methodology has not yet been updated to reflect those changes, including rules addressing used cooking oil and other feedstocks. Among other changes, the law:

Requires emissions rates to exclude emissions attributable to indirect land use change;

Limits eligible transportation fuel to fuel derived exclusively from feedstocks produced or grown in the United States, Mexico or Canada;

Prohibits negative emissions rates, except for transportation fuel derived from animal manure; and

Requires distinct emissions rates for transportation fuels derived from specific animal manure feedstocks.

Background

The Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit, as modified by the WFTC, provides a tax credit for eligible clean transportation fuels produced domestically and sold in a qualified sale, including sustainable aviation fuel and other clean fuels. The credit amount generally depends on a fuel's lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate, with lower-emission fuels qualifying for larger credits.

Today's notice provides the 2026 emissions rate table used to calculate the credit and allows certain regenerative agricultural practices and farm-specific manure management practices to be reflected in emissions calculations, helping agricultural producers participate in the growing domestic biofuels market.

For agricultural feedstocks, the guidance allows taxpayers to account for qualifying low-carbon agricultural practices consistent with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s technical guidelines and the 45Z-specific Feedstock Carbon Intensity Calculator. The guidance also provides transition relief for fuel produced in 2025 and 2026 from certain requirements relating to the development of a nutrient budget before nutrients are applied.

The guidance provides for distinct emissions rates for transportation fuel derived from specific animal manure feedstocks, as required by the WFTC. The 2026 emissions rate table includes dairy manure and swine manure, and Treasury and IRS anticipate that the 45ZCF-GREET model will be updated later in 2026 to include poultry manure and beef manure as primary feedstocks. The guidance also allows farm-specific prior manure management practices to be taken into account in certain circumstances, allowing emissions calculations to better reflect conditions on individual farms.

text:
Brazil needs to do more to convince consumers of ethanol’s benefits if it wants to boost demand for the biofuel, according to Kristell Guizouarn, global sustainability director at Tereos Group.

“I think we need to do some pedagogy to explain that ethanol has a major role to play in energy transition”, said Guizouarn.

Consumer skepticism in Brazil today resembles attitudes toward biofuels in France 15 years ago, Guizouarn said in an interview with The AgriBiz. That poses a challenge in a country where about 85% of the vehicle fleet is flex-fuel but ethanol demand has struggled to respond even when prices are competitive with gasoline.

Sign up The AgriBiz Weekly, a newsletter for global investors

“People used to say, ‘It will damage our engines’ or ‘It will have a negative impact,'” Guizouarn said. “That’s behind us in Europe. The work done over the years has shown there were no technical problems with cars. I think we need to educate consumers and explain that.”

The case for ethanol should increasingly focus on its role in decarbonization and as an alternative to fossil fuels, she said. In France, that message came from several parts of the industry, including automakers.

E85, a fuel blend containing 85% ethanol, is now used in parts of France, where Guizouarn said consumers increasingly associate it with environmental benefits.

“People who use this fuel do so because they believe it has a significant environmental impact,” she said. “They are very proud of it.”

Tereos is France’s largest ethanol producer, the second-largest in Europe and one of the biggest producers in Brazil.

But winning over consumers is only one part of the company’s strategy. Tereos is also seeking to lower the carbon footprint of the ethanol it produces, potentially increasing its value as regulators and customers put a greater premium on lower-emission fuels.

In Europe, that push is being accelerated by the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive, known as RED III, which sets rules and targets for renewable energy use. The revised framework creates incentives for biofuels with lower carbon footprints, an opportunity Tereos is monitoring.

Decarbonization Push

Tereos has been working since at least 2022 on decarbonization targets covering both agricultural and industrial operations globally.

The company set a target in 2022 to cut greenhouse-gas emissions from its agro operations by 32% by 2032. It had achieved a 24% reduction by the 2025/26 season. For industrial operations, the target is a 50% reduction — Tereos has already reached 17%.

Tereos’ farming model differs significantly between Brazil and Europe. In Brazil, the company farms 170,000 hectares (420,000 acres) of land it controls and sources sugarcane from partners covering another 122,000 hectares (301,000 acres). In Europe, it buys crops from growers rather than farming the land itself.

Globally, the cooperative has about 10,000 farmer members, most of them French sugar-beet growers.

In Europe, Tereos has introduced a voluntary regenerative-agriculture program that has attracted about 10% of its farmer members. The five-year program provides technical and financial support.

“We also pay a premium in Europe to farmers who commit to improving their management practices to reduce emissions and who manage to improve their indicators,” Guizouarn said.

Tereos does not yet pay Brazilian growers a premium for cutting emissions, but it has been expanding regenerative practices in the country.

About two-thirds of the roughly 300,000 hectares (741,000 acres) managed by Tereos in Brazil use some form of regenerative practice, according to Felipe Mendes, the company’s sustainability director in the country. Vinasse, a sugarcane-processing byproduct used as fertilizer, is applied to 75% of the area, with a target of 85% by 2030.

Tereos has also been selecting improved sugarcane varieties and expanding the use of biological farm inputs, which now cover about half of its Brazilian acreage.

Those measures have helped make the company’s operations more resilient to extreme weather, Mendes said.

“It was a learning curve that paid off,” he said. “If we go back to 2021/22, we lost 25% of our production that season. Last year, even with a very severe drought, the loss was 10%.”

Tereos is also transferring sustainability practices developed in Brazil to other markets. In Indonesia, where the company has begun buying corn to process into starches and sweeteners, it adapted a monitoring system developed by Brazilian agricultural technology startup Agrotools to assess the crop’s sustainability.

Adding Value to Ethanol

Tereos is also looking beyond road transportation as it seeks new sources of demand for ethanol.

Europe has set a target for sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, to account for 6% of aviation fuel by 2030. Tereos is positioning itself in the alcohol-to-jet market, a process that can convert ethanol into SAF.

In June, the company formed a joint venture with Airbus, Safran and Technip aimed at producing 160,000 metric tons of SAF by 2030.

“We know there will be increasing electrification of road transport in Europe, but we will still have biofuels available,” Guizouarn said. “So how do we prepare the next generation of value for that ethanol? We believe SAF is a good way to do that, and we are studying that possibility in other regions as well.”

text:
HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital Inc., a leading investor in sustainable infrastructure assets, and Burnham, a developer, owner, and operator of wastewater treatment and reuse infrastructure, on Aug. 18 announced the closing of a structured equity investment in the Pasco Resource Recovery Center, a wastewater treatment and reuse facility serving the City of Pasco in Washington State.

Developed, owned, and operated by Burnham, the Pasco Center provides wastewater treatment and reuse services for seven local industrial food-processing plants. The facility uses anaerobic digestion to break down organic matter in wastewater and has the capacity to recycle more than one billion gallons of water annually for agricultural irrigation. In addition to generating reusable water, the Pasco Center also produces renewable natural gas (“RNG”) as a saleable byproduct. The facility further supports resource recovery by producing nutrient-rich soil amendments.

As a partnership between Burnham and the City of Pasco, the Pasco Center replaced Pasco’s original Process Water Reuse Facility in 2025, significantly increasing its wastewater processing capacity and reducing its environmental impact. Output from the upgraded facility is used to irrigate 1,900 acres of agricultural fields owned by the City of Pasco.

HASI’s investment, which closed in July 2026, marks its first transaction in water infrastructure and reflects the company’s continued focus on sustainable infrastructure assets with long-term, contracted cash flows and measurable environmental benefits. The investment is supported by a 30-year wastewater treatment agreement with the City of Pasco.

“HASI is excited to invest in this innovative facility, which not only returns clean water for agricultural use, improves air quality, and reduces emissions in the Pasco area, but also produces RNG to decarbonize the local economy,” said Annmarie Reynolds, HASI’s co-chief investment officer. “We look forward to investing further into water infrastructure and broadening our impact.”

“The Pasco Center is exactly the kind of project Burnham was built to deliver — turning a wastewater challenge into clean, reusable water and a source of renewable energy for the community,” said Chris Tynan, Burnham’s CEO. “HASI’s investment positions us to bring similar solutions to other public utilities facing water and wastewater challenges. We see this as a strong first step with HASI, and we are optimistic there will be more opportunities to partner as our platform continues to grow.”

text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ (Army Corps) announced a Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Sept. 4, seeking public input on additional regulatory language for defining “waters of the United States” (WOTUS) within the 2025 proposed rule.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the announcement “reflects a commitment to radical transparency in developing a durable, final WOTUS definition” that adheres to the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Sackett v. EPA limiting the federal government’s jurisdiction over waters and wetlands covered by the Clean Water Act.

Once finalized, the rule will provide greater predictability for landowners, farmers, energy producers, and small businesses while cutting bureaucratic red tape and protecting water, according to Zeldin.

The announcement was applauded by American Farm Bureau Federation President Zippy Duvall, noting “farmers share the goal of protecting the nation’s natural resources and we’re pleased the EPA and Army Corps put forward a new Waters of the U.S. rule.”

“It respects farmers’ ability to responsibly use their land while ensuring regulations align with the framework established by the Supreme Court’s Sackett ruling,” Duvall continued. “The new WOTUS rule provides a clear understanding of federal jurisdiction, which is critical for farmers who may face severe penalties or even jail time for unknowingly violating the law.”

Proposed supplemental WOTUS

The additional regulatory options for consideration include a proposed definition of “perennial” and alternatives for defining “relatively permanent” and “continuous surface connection.”

Specifically, the agencies are seeking comment on:

Defining “perennial” in the regulatory text to mean “having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions” or, alternatively, to mean “surface water flowing continuously year-round,” consistent with the 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule.

Defining “relatively permanent” to focus on those waters that are perennial bodies of water, except during anomalous events such as drought or dry spell or due to a non-anomalous event resulting in temporary interruption for no more than 30 consecutive days in any given year such as low tide or a regularly occurring dry spell.

Defining “continuous surface connection” to mean perennial surface water in a wetland that is continuously connected with the surface water in the jurisdictional water such that it is difficult to determine where the jurisdictional water ends and the wetland begins, with an exception for temporary interruptions in the surface water connection as the result of anomalous events such as drought or dry spell or a temporary interruption in the surface water connection lasting no more than 30 consecutive days in any given year as a result of non-anomalous events such as low tide or a regularly occurring dry spell.

As an alternative, revising the current category of jurisdictional waters for adjacent wetlands to include only wetlands that are indistinguishably part of a traditional navigable water, the territorial seas, a jurisdictional impoundment, or a jurisdictional tributary. This alternative would also result in deleting the definition of “adjacent.”

While WOTUS determines where federal permits are required for certain activities, waters that fall outside federal jurisdiction remain subject to regulation under state, Tribal, and local law, consistent with the framework that underlies the Clean Water Act, according to EPA Assistant Administrator Water Jessica Kramer.

READ NEXT: EPA RETAINS BIOFUEL DEMAND IN REFINERY EXEMPTIONS, MARKETS, FARM AND FUEL GROUPS RESPOND

“Our goal remains through this process to cut bureaucratic red tape and protect water quality while recognizing that states and tribes truly know their waters best,” Kramer said.

“We want to be sure that we don't have issues related to something called ‘logical outgrowth,’” Kramer added, in hopes of avoiding legal challenges to the final rule “by not having put the public on notice that we were considering alternative options that were not presented in the proposed rule.”

The EPA and Army Corps will accept public comments on the supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking for 30 days once it is published in the Federal Register. Details about commenting can be found on EPA’s Waters of the United States website.

The agencies plan to take final action on the rulemaking after considering comments on the supplemental notice along with the comments received on the 2025 proposed rule.

text:
Most airports can point to a net zero target and a master plan. Far fewer can say, with confidence, what either one will cost, or whether the assumptions behind it still hold.

That gap is no longer a technical footnote. It has become a capital allocation problem, and it is landing squarely on the desks of CEOs and boards rather than sustainability or projects teams.

Two separate pressures are converging at once. On the sustainability side, pledges made back in 2019 and 2020 are now coming due, and the easy part is already behind most airports.

Scope 1 and 2 emissions, the ones an airport directly controls, are the more manageable half of the equation. Scope 3, covering airlines, ground handlers, concessionaires and surface transport, is a different problem entirely: airports have almost no direct authority here, only influence, and that influence is proving thinner than public commitments suggested.

On the infrastructure side, the twenty-year master plan is under similar strain. Demand forecasts that once felt stable are now vulnerable to climate policy shifts, fuel prices, and changing traveller behaviour, all of which can move faster than a runway or terminal can be built.

Add to that the reality of building major infrastructure while an airport keeps operating at full capacity, and the room for error narrows considerably.

Real-world examples already illustrate how airports are approaching these trade-offs. Heathrow Airport has embedded carbon reduction into its long-term capital programme by integrating sustainability requirements into major infrastructure projects, while Cochin International Airport has demonstrated the value of phased investment, expanding from a 12 MW solar plant in 2015 to more than 50 MW today and generating surplus renewable energy for the state grid.

On Scope 3 emissions, San Francisco International Airport’s Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Stakeholder Working Group shows what meaningful collaboration looks like when an airport cannot mandate change but can

Denver International Airport’s Great Hall renovation tells the harder story. A 1.8 billion dollar, 34-year partnership to renovate a live terminal ran into concrete defects and mounting change orders within a year, eventually forcing Denver to terminate the contract, absorb a costly unwind, and rebuild under direct owner control.

The project ultimately succeeded, but only after the airport learned firsthand how much design certainly needs to be locked down before signing a fixed-price contract on a live site.

These are the exact trade-offs the IAS 2026 Roundtables are built around: funding decarbonisation in full versus phasing it, pushing on Scope 3 versus focusing on what’s directly controllable, and committing to infrastructure now versus waiting for more certainty.

None of these have a universal answer. They depend on funding structure, regulatory context and risk appetite, which is exactly why they are better worked through with peers than resolved alone.

Delegates joining the roundtables in Rome this November will leave with a realistic cost baseline for decarbonisation, a clearer read on where Scope 3 influence actually ends, hard lessons from infrastructure delivery gone wrong, and a stronger framework for making capital decisions when the future they’re built for is far from settled.

text:
UK sustainable aviation fuel developer Nova Pangaea Technologies has successfully completed extended trials at its Teesside demonstration plant, strengthening the validation of its technology to convert waste biomass into sustainable aviation fuel. The trials, using softwood residues from timber processing, achieved stable operation for up to 72 hours and delivered yields above the company’s targets, Green Air reported.

The company said the trials used softwood residues from timber processing and demonstrated stable, continuous operation for production runs of up to 72 hours. The trials also delivered yields above the company’s targets.

Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet under Project Speedbird to develop carbon-negative aviation fuel using locally available waste biomass. The company plans to build four facilities in the UK to produce bioethanol that can subsequently be converted into SAF.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts waste biomass and residues, including wood chips, sawdust and wheat straw, into ethanol. The ethanol can be used to produce SAF and renewable diesel. The process also generates biochar, which can permanently store carbon. According to the company, this could allow the overall process to remove more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than it emits.

During the latest trials, Nova Pangaea conducted several production runs using up to three tonnes of feedstock a day. The trials followed smaller-scale tests carried out in early 2025, which demonstrated that the process could operate successfully beyond laboratory conditions.

The company plans to conduct further trials next year to refine the design of its first commercial-scale facility.

“The latest trials have validated our technology and should further underpin the confidence of investors on our journey towards building this first commercial plant,” said Stewart Stewart, who became Nova Pangaea’s CEO earlier this year after working at New York-based investment bank Javelin Capital, where he advised on green fuel opportunities.

The company said it has raised more than £21 million ($28 million) from investors including International Airlines Group, PXN Ventures, Mercia Ventures and the first Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund. It has also received government grant funding through the Advanced Fuels Fund competition.

Stewart said using the UK’s available waste biomass could help increase SAF production while strengthening energy security and creating a new domestic industry.

“By tapping into the plentiful supplies of waste biomass, we can boost SAF production – enhancing our energy security and building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and revenues while reducing fossil fuel emissions,” he said.

Project Speedbird targets 90,000 tonnes annually

Project Speedbird is expected to eventually produce 90,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel a year. Nova Pangaea estimates that the project could reduce net carbon dioxide emissions by up to 541,800 tonnes annually on a lifecycle basis.

British Airways is a founding investor and shareholder in LanzaJet, a US-based SAF producer. LanzaJet’s technology converts second-generation ethanol made from materials such as agricultural residues and woody biomass into aviation fuel and will be used as part of Project Speedbird.

Meanwhile, the UK Department for Transport has published an updated list of feedstocks that qualify under the country’s SAF Mandate. The list includes wastes and residues that can be used to produce eligible low-carbon fuels and is divided into categories, with the names and descriptions of the materials provided.

The department’s updated feedstock list provides further clarity on the types of waste and residue materials that can qualify under the UK’s SAF policy.
